articles.title: Lane Kiffin Uses Viral Fake Quote From Kentucky QB in Photo to Motivate LSU for SEC Matchup
articles.summary: Athletes and coaches have been using slights, real or imagined, as motivation for almost as long as sports have been around.
articles.body:
Athletes and coaches have been using slights, real or imagined, as motivation for almost as long as sports have been around.

And it seems like LSU head coach Lane Kiffin is using an imagined slight ahead of Saturday's game against Kentucky.

It appears as if Kiffin and the Tigers have a quote from Wildcats quarterback Kenny Minchey that says, "LSU's defense hasn't seen anyone like us and our offensive line yet," on their video boards in the facility:

Top Overreactions after Week 5 of CFB Season 😧

The only problem is, Minchey never said that. Adam Luckett of On 3 confirmed he never said as much, but it seems like the Tigers are still using it as motivation.

This isn't the first time Kiffin and LSU decided to use an opposing player's quote as motivation ahead of a game.

He also did so before the matchup with Ole Miss, using a quote from wide receiver Deuce Alexander that said the game was going to be a "bloodbath."

The difference, of course, is that Alexander actually said that. It also likely wasn't hard to get motivated for that matchup with the Rebels considering it was one of the most highly anticipated ones of the season with Kiffin's new team facing his old one.

Ole Miss ended up winning that game, so perhaps a fake quote will work better for Kiffin and Co. when the Tigers face Kentucky.

Facing Minchey will not be easy, so some additional motivation could help. He has completed 68.3 percent of his passes for 1,148 yards, 11 touchdowns and one interception on the season and just put on a show during a dramatic 35-34 overtime victory over South Carolina the last time out.

He threw for 272 yards, three touchdowns and zero interceptions and converted a two-point attempt to win it on the final play.

Both Kentucky and LSU are 4-1 heading into Saturday's matchup. The winner will move up in the SEC standings and still be in the middle of the College Football Playoff race, while the loser will be staring at an uphill battle to get back into those types of postseason discussions.

LSU seems to be pulling out all the stops, including using fake quotes.

articles.title: Group of 6 schools struggling to stay competitive as gap with Power 4 widens: 'It's only going to get harder'
articles.summary: Ever since NIL, revenue sharing and unlimited transfers came to college sports, we've seen evidence suggesting Cinderella might be dying. It's never been mor...
articles.body:
In the aftermath of a close call against Oklahoma last month, New Mexico coach Jason Eck cracked a joke that could probably be considered gallows humor for every coach in the Group of Six.

"Something I'm happy about is we got nine starters on defense who are seniors," Eck said. "So all these SEC coaches will be seeing how good our defense is and they'll look up all those guys they'd like to have play for them and they're going to see they're seniors. They have no eligibility left to transfer to the SEC next year."

Eck's assessment of the current environment in college football was hilariously on the nose. At a place like New Mexico, which has dominated its competition this year outside of that 14-6 loss to the Sooners, the reward for success is power conference programs poring over its film and looking for players they might be able to poach in the transfer portal.

Maybe that's fair. In a world where most people are striving for more money and better career opportunities — including coaches like Eck, whose name will be high on the list for openings when the coaching carousel begins — there's something to be said for college football players having that right as well.

But it's also noticeable how so much roster churn has widened the talent gap between the 68 schools playing power conference football and everyone else, to the point where Group of Six programs sometimes look more like a feeder system than a competitive entity.

In 76 games played this season between the Power Four and the Group of Six, teams from the latter have won just three — a low point in the modern history of college football. But the disparity is even more jarring when you dig into the numbers. Of the 73 wins by power conference teams, only 21 were decided by 14 points or fewer while 27 of those games had a margin of five touchdowns or more. In 10 of those games, the Group of Six team didn't manage to score a single point.

Ever since NIL, revenue sharing and unlimited transfers came to college sports, we have seen bits and pieces of evidence suggesting that Cinderella might be dying in the big-money sports of football and men's basketball. On the heels of a March Madness tournament with no mid-majors in the Sweet 16 and a fairly large sample size on the gridiron this fall, it's getting harder to deny the obvious.

"Let's face reality here," a Group of Six conference source told Yahoo Sports. "The constant cycle of having to reload is brutal. There's not a limitless amount of talent in the system."

Though administrators in those leagues are reluctant to discuss this subject publicly, there's broad acknowledgement that none of this is good for their enterprise.

Despite the financial disparities that have existed for many years, the promise of a MAC program picking off someone in the Big Ten, Memphis upsetting a regional SEC rival or Boise State beating a national power was as much of a tradition as tailgating on Saturday and complaining about the AP poll on Sunday. A handful of programs, like Fresno State, Appalachian State and Georgia Southern, evoked a specific type of fear in power conference fan bases when they showed up on the schedule.

And there's certainly a chance this season is an anomaly. Just a year ago, a dozen power conference teams took a loss to a non-power conference team before the end of September. Two years ago, Notre Dame lost to Northern Illinois and made it to the national championship game.

But when the fact pattern looks like it does this season, even the schools that have enjoyed some success against the power conference teams know there's a potential downside: They're going to get raided.

"The power conference schools are paying backups what we're paying starters," said UMass athletic director Ryan Bamford, who watched his team beat Rutgers in Week 1. "That's a reality. Any time you've got guys that are all-league or putting stuff on tape consistently week in and week out, anyone who's saying that isn't in the back of their mind isn't being truthful."

UMass, which sits at 4-1, is an interesting case study for why that's not necessarily a bad thing. After years of struggling as an FBS independent, which often meant signing up to be power conference cannon fodder so that they could make their budget, Bamford can be choosier about scheduling power conference games as a member of the MAC.

Bamford said that, according to the consultants he uses, the win over Rutgers was worth $40 million in publicity for the school. Even winning the 2021 national championship in men's hockey didn't have that much reach. In a way, it's proof of concept for why so many Group of Six schools keep investing in the football dream, even as they drift further away financially and competitively from the power leagues.

If you can catch that lightning in a bottle one time, it's a supercharger for an entire university.

But if you do it too much, that's a problem as well.

A partial explanation for why there have been fewer Group of Six wins this year is the lack of opportunities for their best teams. With all the power leagues going to nine conference games and potentially being required to play 10 power conference opponents if the playoff expands, why risk another loss?

Boise State, which used to play a lot of big TV games early in the season, went to Oregon last month, has a home-and-home series scheduled with Cincinnati in 2028 and 2029, will play at Washington in 2029 and has a home-and-home with Houston in 2030 and 2031. Arkansas punted a game with Memphis this year to 2030, leaving both the Tigers and USF (the two biggest spenders in the American) without a power conference opponent this season.

UNLV, which only recently became one of the best Mountain West programs, won a home game against Cal last weekend that was scheduled back in 2017 when it sounded like fun to play a road game in Las Vegas. And next year, Arizona State will play at UNLV thanks to another deal signed more than a decade ago. It's no longer going to be that easy now that the Rebels are a regular Group of Six contender.

"The reality is, there are less [power conference teams] scheduling against the G6 in general, and the ones that are, I don't think have the guts to schedule against the best G6 teams," a conference official told Yahoo Sports. "If you look at the matchups, you're not seeing them schedule the better G6 teams nearly as much as they did in the past."

There are no easy fixes for the top Group of Six schools to ensure their continued relevance, but there's incentive on all sides to maintain some version of the status quo where smaller schools make money off big non-conference games and big schools have a proving ground from which they can hire coaches (and now recruit players).

"I think if I learned anything through my time at South Florida, there's no substitute for going and doing it and screwing things up and making it right when there isn't maybe as many eyes on you to where you can learn and gain experience," said Auburn coach Alex Golesh, who parlayed a 9-3 season in the American into an SEC job. "That's invaluable for any of us."

In hopes of patching over some of the holes on Auburn's roster, Golesh brought 13 players with him — 11 on offense, including quarterback Byrum Brown. Though the on-field results have been mixed so far (Auburn is 3-2), these ready-made player/coach packages coming from the Group of Six are going to be the norm as long as the NCAA is unable to enforce any transfer regulations.

"We're kind of leaning into that a little bit like, hey, we're the conference that develops talent," one American Conference athletic director told Yahoo Sports. "Whether that's coaches or athletes or ADs, people want our talent, we develop it and it shows. I think the power conferences need us in kind of a weird way, like we're almost a farm system for them."

Though that's been the case for a few years now, it may finally be starting to show in the on-field results. Those that can get a win over a power conference team better learn to savor it.

"It's only going to get harder," Bamford said, "because the talent disparity is so great."

articles.title: Connor out, Lewis in as England name World Cup squad
articles.summary: Leeds Rhinos half-back Jake Connor is left out of England's Rugby League World Cup squad, with Hull KR's Mikey Lewis beating him to a place.
articles.body:
Jake Connor missed out on a Rugby League World Cup spot by a "small margin" as England seek the players who can best stick to their gameplan, head coach Brian McDermott says.

Leeds Rhinos half-back Connor, the 2025 Super League Man of Steel, was left out of the 23-man squad for the tournament - to be held largely in Australia - with Hull KR's Mikey Lewis making the cut instead.

For Connor, it is another England disappointment to follow his controversial omission from the squad for last autumn's home series against Australia.

"Jake Connor missed out on selection by a small margin and it came down to who I think can best stick to the game plan and attack plan," McDermott said.

The 31-year-old had been expected to make the squad after being talked up by McDermott and enjoying a strong domestic season.

But Hull KR's Lewis, who endured an inconsistent year, has done enough to convince McDermott that he should join captain George Williams, the Warrington stand-off, and Wigan's Harry Smith as half-back options.

England begin their World Cup campaign against Tonga in Perth on 17 October, before facing France in the same city on 24 October and then Papua New Guinea in Wollongong on 30 October.

England squad: Matty Ashton (Warrington Wolves), AJ Brimson (Gold Coast Titans), Ben Currie (Warrington Wolves), Zach Eckersley (Wigan Warriors), Herbie Farnworth (Dolphins), Ethan Havard (Wigan Warriors), Max King (Bulldogs), Morgan Knowles (Dolphins), Mikey Lewis (Hull KR), Jez Litten (Hull KR), Junior Nsemba (Wigan Warriors), Brad O'Neill (Wigan Warriors), Kai Pearce-Paul (Wests Tigers), Victor Radley (Sydney Roosters), Hugo Savala (Sydney Roosters), Harry Smith (Wigan Warriors), Morgan Smithies (Canberra Raiders), Luke Thompson (Wigan Warriors), Sam Walters (Wigan Warriors), Ben Talty (Brisbane Broncos), Jack Welsby (St Helens), George Williams (Warrington Wolves), Dom Young (Newcastle Knights)

There has been much debate about which half-backs would make the England squad after McDermott said last month that he would probably take three to the World Cup, and that captain Williams - who is heading to Australia to join NRL club Dolphins after the tournament - would be one of them.

McDermott said: "Jake has had a really good year. He had an outstanding year last year and got Man of Steel.

"What I've got is a squad full of players who I believe will best play to the game style, the attack plan or game model we identified many weeks ago, that I think we need to compete with the leading nations.

"We can't do the usual things, and I made this a point when I took the job. We've got to play with a point of difference.

"I've got a squad here who I believe are best suited to the attack plan and game model I think England need to play."

Explaining his decision to select Lewis, McDermott added: "I've picked a group of player that have recent history of playing in finals, winning finals, delivering when it matters.

"Mikey Lewis won a World Club Challenge at the start of this year and guided his team to a Challenge Cup final.

"I get he wasn't in the best of shape towards the back of the year and incurred a couple of bans but again, I'll just point people to the attack plan and game model I think England need to have to compete with the leading nations."

Chance for Savala, Wakefield quartet injured

When he replaced Shaun Wane as head coach, McDermott indicated that he was keen to use heritage players - those who qualify for England through family background - to ensure the strongest possible squad.

He has called up two uncapped Australia-born players - versatile back Hugo Savala, part of Sydney Roosters' NRL Grand Final-winning squad, and Brisbane Broncos' front-rower Ben Talty.

Bulldogs prop Max King, born in Huddersfield while his Australian father David was a player there, also earns a first call-up. Victor Radley and AJ Brimson complete the Australia-born contingent in the squad.

Grand Final winners Wakefield have no players in the squad, with Tom Johnstone, Mike McMeeken, Caleb Hamlin-Uele and Jake Trueman all needing time to recover from injuries.

"It's a real shame that the Wakefield boys aren't available," McDermott said. "There's nothing we or they can do. They're all booked in for operations at the end of the year."

And also injured were Sydney Roosters centre Billy Smith - a scorer in Sunday's NRL Grand Final - Wigan centre Jake Wardle, Leeds winger Ash Handley and prop Mikolaj Oledzki, who is leaving Headingley to join NRL side Perth Bears.

Grand Finalists Warrington have three players in the squad - Matty Ashton and Ben Currie joining captain Williams - while Wigan have seven, including Man of Steel winner Brad O'Neill and uncapped centre Zach Eckersley.

Lewis provides off-the-bench spark - analysis

Mikey Lewis over Jake Connor feels like a call made based on pace rather than any other metric, as the Hull KR half is much more of a runner than his opposite number.

He's also perhaps more of an off-the-bench spark than the Leeds playmaker, given George Williams and Harry Smith's blend of run threat and game management will probably get the nod at six and seven.

Herbie Farnworth has been one of the best players in the world for some time and has taken his game to new levels in 2026, and getting the centre involved must be among Brian McDermott's biggest tactical challenges.

Dom Young is another thoroughbred who England will look to out wide, having helped Newcastle to the NRL Grand Final.

Victor Radley's influence and savage tackling makes him a shoo-in for the pack, something that was missed in last year's Ashes series against Australia, and there are other big hitters in the ranks with Morgan Knowles and Morgan Smithies also sharpened by their NRL exploits, and Brad O'Neill back in the international picture after a Man of Steel year.

Staying with the pack, the prospect of a Kai Pearce-Paul and Junior Nsemba second-row pairing whets the appetite.

Elsewhere, the new imports from the NRL have pedigree; Max King has played State of Origin, Hugo Savala can jump into a number of backs spots and Ben Talty is an athletic front-rower who helped Brisbane to success in 2025.

Zach Eckersley has impressed for Wigan this year, and his strong build and athleticism - coupled with an ability to put a winger away - make him a solid inclusion, while Matty Ashton's return after his missed the Ashes with an anterior cruciate knee ligament injury gives England genuine pace out wide.

Everyone will have their opinion on the squad, which features no selections from Super League champions Wakefield - albeit with some contenders unavailable - but there is a balance to the selection.

McDermott has said England might need something different to truly test the best, and it is that conundrum which will again be at the forefront of his thoughts.

Walsh makes Australia squad but faces full-back battle

Reece Walsh has secured a place in Australia's men's World Cup squad, also named on Monday - although head coach Kevin Walters has refused to confirm whether he will be first-choice full-back.

Walsh has struggled to hit the heights of last season, when he inspired Brisbane Broncos to their first NRL Grand Final triumph in 19 years before helping Australia to a 3-0 Test series win over England.

He missed the end of this season to have ankle surgery, but with Penrith's Dylan Edwards ruled out of the World Cup with a knee injury, Walsh will vie for the full-back spot with James Tedesco - man of the match as Sydney Roosters beat Newcastle Knights 19-18 in Sunday's NRL Grand Final.

Loose forward Isaah Yeo will delay surgery on a torn pectoral muscle to captain Australia.

Winger Mark Nawaqanitawase - who scored two tries in Sydney's win on Sunday - is not in the squad because of his impending code switch to union with Japanese side Saitama Wild Knights. Second-row forward Angus Crichton is absent for the same reason, as he is joining NSW Waratahs.

Star half-back Nathan Cleary is out of the tournament with a broken ankle while Lindsay Smith has been added to the squad in place of Lindsay Collins, who misses out with a foot injury.

Australia men's squad: Isaah Yeo (captain), Bradman Best, Jack Bostock, Blake Brailey, Pat Carrigan, Lindsay Smith, Reuben Cotter, Tom Dearden, Tino Fa'asuamaleaui, David Fifita, Harry Grant, Keaon Koloamatangi, Liam Martin, Latrell Mitchell, Mitchell Moses, Cameron Munster, Cameron Murray, Jacob Preston, Kotoni Staggs, James Tedesco, Tom Trbojevic, Sam Walker, Reece Walsh.

Ali Brigginshaw has missed out on the chance to go for a fourth World Cup winners' medal after being omitted from Australia's women's squad.

Head coach Jess Skinner said the 36-year-old Brisbane half-back - Australia's captain when they won the tournament in Manchester four years ago - was "upset" to be left out.

"That was one of the hardest phone calls I've had to make as a coach to a player and to talk about her and where she was," Skinner said.

Australia women's squad: Isabelle Kelly (captain), Tarryn Aiken, Kezie Apps, Shaylee Bent, Jaime Chapman, Abbi Church, Quincy Dodd, Millie Elliott, Tiana Penitani Gray, Olivia Higgins, Ellie Johnston, Keilee Joseph, Jocelyn Kelleher, Olivia Kernick, Keeley Nizza, Sariah Paki, Julia Robinson, Jessica Sergis, Jesse Southwell, Simaima Taufa, Sarah Togatuki, Tamika Upton, Makenzie Weale.

articles.title: Portugal boss Jorge Jesus responds after Cristiano Ronaldo calls him out in controversial statement
articles.summary: Portugal head coach Jorge Jesus has responded to Cristiano Ronaldo after being called out in a 2,000-word statement on Tuesday. The pair fell out during the...
articles.body:
Portugal head coach Jorge Jesus has responded to Cristiano Ronaldo after being called out in a 2,000-word statement on Tuesday. The pair fell out during the recent international break, where Portugal played four Nations League games.

Ronaldo claimed Jesus told him he would play against Norway but left him on the bench as an unused substitute. The Al-Nassr forward then walked out of the team despite Portugal having two more games to play.

Jesus was then expected to clarify the situation in his press conference with an eight-point statement, but he did not follow the script. Ronaldo subsequently posted a lengthy social media message giving his version of events, and Jesus has now responded.

Jorge Jesus responds after Cristiano Ronaldo accuses him of breaking his word

Jorge Jesus took the sensible approach of not adding more fuel to the fire. He chose not to make any controversial comments about Cristiano Ronaldo's accusation that he went back on his word.

Jesus responded: "I read the statement, and now, like I do every day, I'm going to the Federation headquarters to work, to think about the Portuguese national team". "I have nothing more to say."

While Jesus' response was reasonable, it did little to suggest what Ronaldo's international future will be. The 41-year-old is reportedly not prepared to play for the national team until Jesus leaves.

However, Jesus only recently signed a four-year deal that will take him to the 2030 World Cup , which Portugal is co-hosting. This suggests Ronaldo may have played his last game for Portugal, or perhaps only has a farewell appearance remaining.

articles.title: Liga MX side Atlas FC announces new stadium with 2030 opening date
articles.summary: The Guadalajara club will move to nearby Zapopan, where rival Chivas. already play, in an agreement with the Universidad de Guadalajara.
articles.body:
Atlas FC got a new owner. Now, it's getting a new home.

The Guadalajara club, which is celebrating its 110th anniversary this year, announced it will move to nearby Zapopan and anchor a new stadium as part of the Universidad de Guadalajara's Ciudad UdeG district.

The stadium, which is being designed by stadium architecture firm Populous, is expected to open in 2030, ahead of the 2031 Women's World Cup taking place in Mexico, the United States, Costa Rica and Jamaica.

While the intention is for Atlas to be the primary tenant of the stadium with a capacity of more than 40,000, the Leones Negros of U de G, currently in Mexico's second division, also will play its home matches there.

José Miguel Bejos, the president of Grupo PRODI which completed the purchase of Atlas this summer, said at an event unveiling the plans that the stadium will not utilize any public money, and the intention is for it to serve the university community with events on non-matchdays.

"We'll be partners of the Universidad de Guadalajara in a project, thinking about positively transforming its surroundings and creating value for the community over the next decades," he said. "For us, building doesn't end when you inaugurate a building: Whoever builds it stays there and answers for anything openly."

What will happen to the Estadio Jalisco when Atlas moves to its new stadium?

The team will be back at its current stadium, the Estadio Jalisco, for a crosstown rivalry match against Chivas on Saturday, Oct. 10. Chivas also called the Jalisco home before moving to its current stadium in Zapopan in 2010.

That stadium played host to four 2026 World Cup matches, three decades after the Jalisco hosted six matches in the 1986 World Cup. The venue, which current plans call to keep active hosting events, also played host to eight games at the 1970 World Cup.

articles.title: No. 8 Cougars aren’t panicking over their pedestrian passing numbers
articles.summary: Should BYU coaches be concerned that they have the fewest passing yards of any power conference team in college football?
articles.body:
No power conference football team in the country has fewer passing yards this season than BYU, which has only 719 yards through the air through four games.

Does that mean it is time to panic in Provo?

Hardly, BYU quarterback Bear Bachmeier, offensive coordinator Aaron Roderick and passing game coordinator Fesi Sitake said Tuesday as the No. 8 Cougars (4-0, 2-0) prepared to host Iowa State on Friday night (8:15 p.m. MDT, ESPN) at LaVell Edwards Stadium.

"Kind of an anomaly last game (versus TCU)," said Bachmeier. "I am very confident in our pass game. … I mean, we just want to play BYU football. We want to sling the pill around and be physical in the run game, so yeah."

In the 17-10 win over TCU , Bachmeier completed only 11 of 24 passes for 62 yards, as a persistent drizzly rain and misty conditions in Fort Worth made gripping the ball and completing passes extra difficult, the quarterback said.

"It was one of those games," Bachmeier said. "Luckily we got out of there with a win. … We knew it was going to be rainy, and there was a little mist that Saturday, too, but yeah, circumstances arose and I am just proud of the team and how we bounced back."

Bouncing back meant Bachmeier put the outcome of the game on his legs , and rushed for 66 yards and two touchdowns, including the game-sealer from 21 yards out with 2:06 remaining.

"Like, we don't have gaudy stats right now, but they're blocking their butts off. They're doing a great job lining up right, doing what they're supposed to. They're just happy we're winning right now, but they also believe we will hit our stride in the passing game here soon."

Bachmeier and Sitake both brushed back against suggestions that receivers and tight ends weren't getting open against TCU's heavy zone defense in the secondary.

"They found voids (in the coverage), but obviously circumstances arose and we had to adapt," Bachmeier said. "… BYU football is hard-nosed, and we're going to run the ball and we're going to take shots, and be dynamic in the run game and in the pass game."

Asked Monday whether the receivers were struggling to get open against TCU and if that was a concern, head coach Kalani Sitake got right to the point.

Certainly, BYU's run game has been dynamic, which is a major reason why the passing numbers have been pedestrian. As was the case last Saturday and in the second halves against Colorado State and Utah Tech, Roderick called plays designed to milk the clock and get the games over as quickly as possible.

"We do whatever it takes to win here, and that's part of being a team, and it was a tough night. The weather was really bad," Roderick said, while also praising TCU's defense. "… We did have some struggles that were self-inflicted. They were our own problems. That game got to the point where it was just (time to) hunker down and do what you have to do to get out of there with a win."

The Cougars are now 131st in the Football Bowl Subdivision in total passing yards (719) and 114th in passing yards per game (179.8). They are 132nd in pass attempts (89 passes) and 94th in passing touchdowns, with just six.

However, they are still among the more efficient passing teams in the country, averaging 8.1 yards per attempt (47th).

"I've been really pleased with the receivers," Fesi Sitake said. "Like A Rod said, we haven't really had the opportunity to throw the ball a lot. We've seen flashes, and we are excited for the chance to just let it go for four quarters.

That could come as soon as Friday, as BYU is down to its third- and fourth-string running backs, Preston Rex and true freshman Journee Tonga. Roderick said freshman Devaughn Eka could also get some carries this week.

Top running back LJ Martin has been ruled out with an ankle sprain. Martin is averaging 7.8 yards per carry and 86.0 yards per game.

Roderick said the receivers have handled the situation well, noting that nobody is grousing about not seeing the ball enough.

"There was not one long face on our team about our passing stats or who touched the ball or anything," he said. "If you see the final touchdown at the end of the game and the celebration in the end zone, it was a really good sign of what kind of team we have and how much the guys care about each other."

BYU's tight ends — starters Walker Lyons and Roger Saleapaga and reserve Keayen Nead — have combined to catch 13 passes for 131 yards. Saleapaga missed the CSU game and Nead is more of a blocking tight end.

"We just haven't been able to play that much yet," Roderick said. "We had two games where we played half the game and they both had an impact. … And then the Arizona game, I thought they both played well. Then last week that game did not go as planned with the weather.

"I think they're both doing a lot of good things, and you are going to see a lot of them the rest of the year," he continued.

Fesi Sitake has been saying since spring ball came and went without BYU making a move to replace Parker Kingston that he was happy with the makeup of his receivers room . Through four games, he hasn't changed his stance on that, as freshman Legend Glasker and Kyler Kasper have emerged as BYU's top two pass-catchers.

Glasker has 14 catches for 279 yards and two touchdowns, and Kasper has 11 catches for 138 yards and two TDs. Returner Jojo Phillips is off to a slower start, with six catches for 45 yards and one TD.

"The mantra in our room is being committed to the process without being emotionally attached to the results," Sitake said. "The process right now is to do whatever we can to help the team win.

"There are going to be times where we have to throw for 400 yards, and then there's times like we have had this season where we have to run the ball a ton," he continued. "So, we're good. These guys have bought into that message. And they are very aware of the opportunity we have ahead of us."

Snow College transfer Reggie Frischknecht has two catches , while Tiger Bachmeier and Jared Esplin have one each. Sitake said a few other guys are "close" to seeing more playing time, most notably freshmen Jaron Pula and Terrance Saryon and sophomore Tei Nacua.

He said tight ends Saleapaga and Lyons "have a great relationship" and have "put any differences aside" for the good of the team.

"That says a lot about those two," Sitake said. "They celebrate when each other does something well, and that's trickled over into the receivers room. It is just a sign of a great culture, great leadership on this team, and we are glad to have those kinds of guys."

articles.title: As potential Hurricane Isaias forms in the Gulf, Alabama says game vs. Georgia still set to be played as scheduled
articles.summary: The top-10 matchup is set for a 7:30 p.m. ET kickoff. And right now, it looks like a lot of rain is in the forecast.
articles.body:
Alabama said on Wednesday evening that its game against Georgia was set to proceed as scheduled.

A weather system in the Gulf of Mexico has become Tropical Storm Isaias , and will likely be upgraded to a hurricane in the coming days. The track of the storm is currently aimed east of Texas and potentially toward the Gulf Coast of Mississippi and Alabama with potential landfall later in the week.

That means the No. 6 Crimson Tide's home game in Tuscaloosa against the No. 2 Bulldogs on Saturday could be plagued by lots and lots of rain.

"Alabama athletics continues to closely monitor the weather forecast ahead of Saturday's football game, with the safety and well-being of the student-athletes, coaches, staff and fans as our highest priority," the school said in a statement on Wednesday night . "We remain in close communication with the National Weather Service, the Southeastern Conference office and the University of Georgia as we observe conditions. "At this time, kickoff remains scheduled for 6:30 p.m. CT Saturday. We continue to encourage fans to rely on official Alabama athletics and SEC channels for the latest information regarding Saturday's game."

"At this time, kickoff remains scheduled for 6:30 p.m. CT Saturday. We continue to encourage fans to rely on official Alabama athletics and SEC channels for the latest information regarding Saturday's game."

Alabama's statement was similar to one the school put out on Tuesday night. Al.com published a story on Tuesday interviewing meteorologist James Spann, the most widely respected weather voice in the state.

"We've got potential for a hurricane making landfall in Mobile Bay," Spann told the site. "The Alabama-Georgia game, a presidential visit, 'College GameDay.' You got the big [Zach Bryan] concert at Auburn. This is the National Shrimp Festival at Gulf Shores this weekend, which is huge. I mean you could not … it's gonna be a nightmare."

Yes, Spann is referring to President Donald Trump. The president is expected to be in attendance for the game. It's the second SEC game he's attended in three weeks. He was at Texas' win over Tennessee in Week 4. ESPN's pregame show was also in Knoxville for that game.

Kickoff for Saturday's game is set for just after 7:30 p.m. ET on ABC. It's the only matchup of top-10 teams and one of just two matchups between teams in the AP Top 25 in Week 6.
